photo_021.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely notice:

- **Awkward bedroom geometry:** The room is long and narrow, with a projecting/curved soffit or bulkhead along the right side and a beam across the ceiling. It limits furniture placement and makes the space feel more like a converted or reconfigured area than a clean rectangular bedroom.
- **Potentially low/uneven ceiling conditions:** The ceiling drops and boxed-in areas deserve investigation—could simply conceal HVAC, plumbing, or structure, but should be understood before opening walls.
- **Odd door/transom setup:** The closet door with the large transom-like opening above it, plus the nearby open doorway, creates visual clutter. A remodel could simplify this with a full-height closet system, revised door placement, or more cohesive trim.
- **Limited usable wall space:** The windows, closet, hall opening, and unusual ceiling leave relatively little uninterrupted wall area. Built-ins or a more deliberate furniture layout may add value.
- **Dated finishes:** Carpet, basic trim, flush-panel closet door, and the ceiling light fixture are straightforward cosmetic upgrade opportunities.
- **Window/egress and privacy check:** The narrow side windows appear small; confirm bedroom egress, insulation, and privacy treatment if this is being marketed as a bedroom.
- **Possible layout opportunity:** If adjacent hall/closet space permits, there may be an opportunity to improve closet storage or create a more defined primary-suite feel—but the ceiling bulkheads may constrain major changes.

The biggest question is what is inside the soffits/ceiling drops; that determines whether this is mostly a cosmetic refresh or a more involved reconfiguration.

In photo_021 the visible trim is a clean white six-panel colonial door with plain painted casing and a narrow painted baseboard (largely occluded by the bed and nightstand); in photo_023 the window carries a fairly substantial molded white casing with a sill and apron, plus a clean painted baseboard, and the same six-panel door. What 2a did NOT contain is any observation of trim damage, wear, undersizing, or stylistic obsolescence — it supplies no basis for the upgrade framing it asserts; it simply files ordinary, clean painted trim into a dated-finishes bucket. Every later stage carried that unchanged rather than distorting it: 2b produced faithful bullets ("The trim is basic." / "The room has beige walls, carpet, basic trim, and a simple interior door.") joined exact, 2c kept both, 2d resolved both to dated_interior_trim via exact_kind — a correct catalog mapping of "basic trim" — the issues projected to one condition, and Terra supported it. prior_attribution.p2a_excerpt: The gray raised-panel cabinet and mixed hardware feel transitional/dated next to the contemporary faucet.
prior_attribution.rationale:
STEP 1 — premise confirmed. The billed claim is condition oc1_c0372aa08127c1f1, catalog item vanity_dated_style (kind modernization), claim text "bathroom vanity dated style, functional", disposition accepted_for_work. Photo_025 shows a bathroom that has plainly just been renovated: a gray raised-panel vanity with a clean white stone-look top, undamaged doors and drawer fronts, a contemporary matte-black faucet and towel ring, a large framed mirror, fresh neutral paint, new LVP flooring and new baseboard. Photo_031 shows a second, equally fresh bath: white raised-panel vanity, white counter, black faucet, dark-framed mirror, chrome bar light, and a fully modern dark large-format tiled shower with hex mosaic floor and a linear drain. Nothing in either photo shows a dated, worn, damaged, or obsolete vanity — the cabinetry is new-looking and part of the same recent update as the rest of each room. "Raised panel" is a door profile, not evidence of datedness. So the human v1.1 adjudication (claim absent, work none, hard_false_billed) holds on my own inspection: this is a taste preference billed as a condition, not a photo-supported defect.

STEP 2 — the unsupported material claim already exists in the 2a prose, so 2a is the first stage that went wrong. Photo_025's 2a prose contains a dedicated bullet, "Vanity is the main style mismatch," asserting the cabinet and hardware "feel transitional/dated" and recommending painting, hardware swaps, or a new vanity to "modernize it quickly." Photo_031's 2a prose independently asserts "Mixed design eras," calling the white raised-panel vanity, counter, mirror and light "builder-grade/traditional" and recommending "Updating the vanity/mirror/light." What the 2a prose did NOT contain is any observed defect: photo_025's own prose explicitly states there are "no apparent signs of water damage, cracked finishes, or major deterioration," and photo_031 describes the room as a "recent cosmetic bathroom update." So 2a supplied the exact false meaning that was ultimately billed — "dated," warranting modernization — with no defect behind it.

Every later stage carried that meaning faithfully rather than distorting it: 2b joined all three issues by exact method (bullets 6, 7, 9 restating the same prose claims), 2c retained them, 2d resolved all three to vanity_dated_style by exact_kind (routing_reason exact_kind, so no mis-resolution), 2e kept all three (removed_count 0, no suppression reasons), projection produced the single condition, and Terra supported it with a rationale ("raised-panel vanity cabinetry with traditional styling") that is merely restating 2a's premise. No downstream stage introduced anything 2a had not already asserted, so downstream attribution is not available; the first responsible stage is 2a itself.

prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise confirmed. The photo shows a dark, high-gloss plank floor whose grain repeats photographically board-to-board (laminate/LVP rather than solid hardwood), and the foreground third shows light streaks along board edges, mismatched lighter boards toward the bottom-left, and seam lines catching light — consistent with the adjudicated v1.1 verdict (claim=exact, work=warranted, terra_claim_supported). A real, billable flooring condition went unbilled.

The 2a prose DID contain the condition, and contained it specifically: it names the flooring bullet as "heavily worn/scuffed" and as appearing "to have lifting/open seams or patched areas near the foreground" — both the material read ("dark plank") and the defect ("lifting/open seams") are present, so pass_2a is not the failure. What 2a did NOT contain was a material identification as vinyl/linoleum; it said only "dark plank flooring."

Walking the ladder: 2b produced the matching bullet ("Flooring has lifting or open seams near the foreground.") and the join is exact, so not 2b. p2c_dropped is empty and the bullet appears in p2c_surviving, so not 2c. 2d resolved it to vinyl_linoleum_torn_or_lifted; that resolution is endorsed rather than faulted by the truth basis, because the human graded the claim axis "exact" against that item's claim text ("vinyl or linoleum flooring torn, worn through, or lifting material") — so 2d is not the first wrong stage. p2e_status is "kept" and, per the corpus rule, 2e is not an available attribution anyway. The issue did become a condition (projected_condition_id oc1_476cd4f80565d162), so condition_projection is not it.

That leaves Terra, which is where it actually died: terra_verdict "unsupported", terra_rationale "The visible flooring is hard plank material, with no vinyl or linoleum tears, lifting, or open seams shown", disposition excluded with reason_code verdict_unsupported and accepted=false. Terra rejected a claim the human adjudicated as supported, and it did so on material-identity grounds — asserting the plank material is not vinyl/linoleum — which the photo does not establish (the repeating grain and gloss are at least as consistent with LVP as with hardwood) and which the human's own note flags as a catalog-vocabulary trap ("we might want to change the catalog to 'hard flooring' ... so that we dont get caught up on hardwood, LVP, linoleum"). Note also that Terra's rationale goes further and denies "lifting, or open seams" outright, contradicting the 2a observation and the foreground evidence. This is not the known post-Terra routing gap: Terra did not support this condition, it rejected it, so the ladder has a rung that fits.

- **Countertops/backsplash:** Dark laminate-style counters and the lack of a backsplash are the clearest dated elements. New quartz/solid-surface counters plus a tile or slab backsplash would make a major visual difference.
- **Layout constraints:** It is a narrow galley/L-shaped workspace with limited continuous prep area, especially around the range and small sink. Any major renovation should assess whether adjacent space can be borrowed or whether a slimmer range/sink configuration improves usability.
- **Appliances:** The stainless gas range and over-the-range microwave are relatively modern and likely reusable, although the microwave dominates the upper-cabinet area. A vent hood could be a more upscale replacement if venting is feasible.
- **Sink/window area:** The small sink and basic faucet are prime upgrade items. The window provides welcome light, but the exterior door nearby limits wall/cabinet flexibility.
- **Floors:** Hardwood flooring is a positive and worth protecting/refinishing if needed.
- **Finishing details:** Uneven-looking cabinet-bottom trim, older blinds, basic lighting, and neutral walls suggest straightforward finishing work could noticeably elevate the room.

Overall: **good candidate for a moderate cosmetic renovation**, but a full transformation would require careful planning because the room’s footprint and door/window placement limit expansion.

prior_attribution.p2a_excerpt: The wood porch, railings, stair stringers, and handrails show weathering and likely need repair or replacement.
prior_attribution.rationale: Premise confirmed. Photos 017 and 028 show one raised rear wood deck reached by a long exterior wood stair: bare grey weathered decking with raised grain and worn board edges, stair treads and stringers greyed and heavily worn, a dark-stained board ceiling overhead. Real work is warranted, but the billed name ("patio or porch surface aging, surface wear, or coating breakdown") names a surface/coating mechanism on a patio-or-porch surface, while the visible mechanism is bare-wood weathering and deterioration of decking and stair treads calling for board replacement. (Photo_001 shows only marble stoops on a rowhouse front, no porch at all, so one of the three evidence legs is spurious as well.) Attribution: 2a is not responsible. Its prose contained the correctly-named problem in fuller form on both porch photos -- photo_028: "The wood porch, railings, stair stringers, and handrails show weathering and likely need repair or replacement," plus a separate rot/footing inspection note; photo_017: "Floorboards are heavily weathered and may have splitting/cupping. Expect possible board replacement and checking joists, ledger attachment, and footings." What 2a did NOT contain anywhere is the word or notion of a patio surface, a coating, or coating breakdown; nothing in any of the three proses attributes the wear to a finish failing. 2b preserved both object and mechanism verbatim in kind ("The wood front porch is weathered", "The porch floorboards are heavily weathered") -- it thinned the detail (dropping splitting/cupping and the structural-rot bullet entirely) but introduced no wrong name, and 2c kept both bullets. The mislabel is first introduced at 2d, the stage that actually chooses the name: it mapped a true generic wood-weathering bullet onto catalog item patio_or_porch_surface_wear (resolution_path llm, 7 candidates, routing_reason exact_kind), swapping wood deterioration for surface/coating wear. Condition projection and Terra then inherited that name -- Terra's own rationale echoes it ("clear weathering and surface wear") -- so neither is the first fault. Confidence is medium rather than high because the three sibling bullets on photo_028 (railings, stair stringers, handrails weathered) resolved to catalog_item_id null, which hints the catalog may lack a wood deck/stair deterioration item; if so 2d picked the closest available name rather than freely choosing a wrong one. The ladder has no catalog-gap rung, and 2d owns the naming decision, so 2d is the answer.

- **Old or compromised exterior finishes.** The horizontal siding is aged and stained, while trim around the windows and door looks tired. Expect scraping/repair at minimum; replacement may be more economical in affected areas.
- **Windows and rear door appear dated.** The multi-pane windows/sunroom-style enclosure and basic rear door are likely inefficient and may need replacement or rebuilding depending on condition.
- **Masonry/chimney needs inspection.** The exposed brick chimney and adjacent wall look generally intact from this distance, but flashing, mortar joints, and moisture intrusion should be checked—especially given the roof condition.
- **Major site cleanup.** A large fallen tree/log, overgrowth, debris, and old patio contents indicate immediate cleanup, hauling, and landscaping work. Confirm whether the tree affected fencing, utilities, drainage, or the structure.
- **Patio and retaining planters need rebuilding.** The hardscape is neglected, uneven-looking, and cluttered. The low brick planters/retaining walls may be salvageable but likely need re-pointing or replacement.
- **Drainage is a concern.** The patio sits close to the house, with exposed soil and signs of neglect along the foundation line. A renovator would check slope, downspout discharge, and whether water is being directed away from the house.

Photo_016 shows a brick-paver rear patio that is genuinely aged, darkened, soiled and buried under dead leaves, twigs and yard debris next to a felled tree — a real problem, and rebuild/clean work is warranted. photo_025.jpg.p2a_prose:
To a renovator, this looks more like a cosmetic-refresh room than a major rehab—assuming the unseen systems and structure check out.

- **Good fundamentals:** Decent room size, a large window for natural light, and what appears to be intact plaster/drywall and ceiling.
- **Dated finishes:** Beige walls, basic white trim, older-looking radiator, and mixed flooring/rugs make it feel visually dated.
- **Flooring opportunity:** The carpet/rug combination is the biggest immediate update candidate. Pulling it up could reveal usable original flooring—or create a clean slate for new LVP/hardwood/carpet.
- **Radiator consideration:** It is functional-looking but visually intrusive. A renovator may refinish it, add a radiator cover, or assess whether a heating upgrade is worthwhile.
- **Window/trim:** The window itself appears serviceable, but the curtain hardware and trim treatment are dated. Check for drafts, operation, and any moisture staining around the opening.
- **Paint and prep:** Walls look generally sound but likely need patching, caulk at trim, and a modern paint palette. The visible small marks/scuffs suggest routine prep work.
- **Layout:** Bed placement is workable, though the room feels crowded by the oversized furniture. Built-in or more streamlined storage could improve circulation.

The paint film is intact: no peeling, no bubbling, no flaking at corners or baseboard, no patchy nicotine-style discoloration or aged/uneven finish. So the billed claim "interior paint peeling, bubbling, or visibly aged finish" (accepted_for_work, degradation) is unsupported, matching the adjudicated v1.1 axes (claim absent / work none).

What the 2a prose DID contain: a single mention of the walls, "yellowed wall color", placed inside the list headed "Dated finishes are the main opportunity" alongside "old light fixture, ornate mirror, ceiling treatment" — all style/vintage items, framed as things that "can be transformed relatively quickly." Read in that context it is a dated-palette observation about the wall's hue, which the photo genuinely supports. The prose also carries one hedged condition remark, "likely aging paint/trim," which 2b captured as its own bullet ("Paint and trim are likely aging.") and 2c DROPPED — it is not this condition's lineage.

What the 2a prose did NOT contain: any assertion of peeling, bubbling, flaking, damaged or visibly degraded paint. Its overall reading is "good bones, cosmetic upside," and where it does flag condition (floor wear) it says "nothing obviously alarming from the photo." So the material false claim does not already appear at 2a, which rules out pass_2a.

2b joined exactly ("Wall color is yellowed.", bullet_index 5, method exact) and preserved the color reading verbatim; 2c kept that bullet — keeping a true observation is not the error. The meaning flips at 2d: resolution chose peeling_or_discolored_paint from 6 candidates via the llm path, an item whose claim template asserts "interior paint peeling, bubbling, or visibly aged finish." That is the first stage where a true dated-color observation became a false paint-degradation defect; note its sibling from the same 2a sentence ("The light fixture is old.") correctly landed as modernization. condition_projection only instantiated the catalog item's claim text, and Terra then rubber-stamped it with its own invented detail ("visibly uneven, discolored areas"), but both are downstream of the wrong-item resolution. 2e is not available (issue is in kept_issue_ids and produced a condition regardless).

Confidence is medium, not high, for two reasons: (a) "yellowed" can be read as age-discoloration rather than hue, which would push the error up to 2a — I resolved it toward hue because of the "Dated finishes" framing and the style-item company it keeps; (b) the p2c_surviving entry already carries kind "degradation", and 2d's routing_reason is "exact_kind", so if that kind label is genuinely authored at 2c then 2c pre-committed the defect framing and would be the first responsible stage. The record's per_issue block attributes the item choice to 2d (resolution_path llm, candidate_count 6), so 2d is the best-supported call from the evidence available.

A renovator would likely see a **functional but highly dated, narrow galley kitchen** with clear cosmetic upside—and possible layout constraints.

- **Mixed, piecemeal finishes.** White cabinets, older laminate counters, a small newer-looking mosaic backsplash, open shelving, and varied appliances create an unfinished/remodeled-in-stages appearance.
- **Cabinet condition and storage.** Existing cabinets appear serviceable but dated, with worn edges and inconsistent units. Replacing or refacing them could make a dramatic difference; full-height cabinetry may improve storage if ceiling height and clearances allow.
- **Countertop and backsplash opportunity.** Counters look like older laminate and have visible wear. A continuous countertop/backsplash package would substantially modernize the room.
- **Lighting is weak.** A single central ceiling fixture leaves work areas underlit. Recessed or slim surface lighting plus under-cabinet lighting would be a high-impact upgrade.
- **Flooring is dated and appears worn.** The sheet/vinyl-style flooring looks tired; replacement with durable LVP or tile could visually unify the kitchen and hall.
- **Walls/paint need attention.** Visible scuffs, patchy areas, and generally tired finishes suggest prep, repair, and repainting throughout.
- **Appliance/ventilation review.** The electric range and hood appear basic/older; a renovator would check whether the hood vents outside or recirculates, and confirm electrical capacity before changing appliances.
- **Potentially awkward circulation.** Doors/openings on the right side and the hall beyond may limit cabinet depth, island options, and appliance placement.

**Positive:** There is a usable run of cabinetry, a dedicated cooking zone, and some evidence of prior updates. A focused cosmetic renovation—new cabinets or fronts, counters, flooring, paint, lighting, and coordinated appliances—could materially improve it without necessarily moving plumbing.

prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise confirmed by direct inspection: masonry weathering/discoloration is plainly real across this property, and it is not only stone. photo_023 shows a genuine BRICK Tudor house whose tall brick chimney stack carries heavy dark vertical staining, plus a brick retaining wall and a stained/parged wall below the porch; photo_014 and photo_034 show a sandstone facade and chimney with dark staining, biological growth and worn joints; photo_035 shows discolored/moss-stained stone with patched mortar; photo_002/photo_022 show a heavily moss-stained, spalled masonry grill. The condition "brickwork weathering or discoloration" is supported, and the human adjudication (claim=exact, work=warranted) is the authority here.

The 2a prose is not the failure point: it contains the condition explicitly on four of the six photos — photo_014 "Heavy staining/weathering and potentially deteriorated mortar joints", photo_023 "The tall brick stack shows weathering", photo_034 "the chimney and some wall areas show dark staining, weathering", photo_035 "There appear to be patched/repointed areas, discoloration". What 2a did NOT contain is any claim that the mortar is intact — it repeatedly said the opposite (deteriorated/uneven mortar joints, repointing needed) — but that is a detail of the catalog item's claim wording, not an absence of the condition.

Every later stage carried it forward intact: all seven issues joined to a 2b bullet by exact match, all seven survived 2c (p2c_present true), 2d resolved each to brick_weathered_or_discolored via exact_kind, all were kept by 2e, and all seven projected to the single condition oc1_fd62a1d71743be6b, which reached Terra. So 2b, 2c, 2d, condition_projection and 2e all did their job (and per the record 2e never costs a condition in this corpus).

Terra is the first and only stage that went wrong: it returned "unsupported" on a condition whose substance it conceded — "The visible masonry is heavily stained and weathered, but it is stone rather than brick and some joints appear deteriorated" — rejecting on the catalog item's material/mortar wording rather than on whether the weathering exists. That rejection is what unbilled it (accepted=false, reason_code verdict_unsupported, disposition excluded), and photo_023 shows actual brick with weathering and intact mortar, so even the literal wording had support. This is not the post-Terra routing gap: Terra did not support the condition, it rejected it.

I considered 2d — picking a brick-named item for evidence that is mostly stone is what set Terra's objection up — but the adjudicated truth basis records the claim axis as "exact", meaning the resolved item's claim matches the photos, so 2d did not go wrong by the governing authority.

- **Basement-level opportunity and concern:** The visible lower-level windows suggest usable basement space, but also raise questions about waterproofing, ceiling height, egress, foundation condition, and whether it can legally be finished or rented.

Premise confirmed on my own reading of both photos. Photo_008 (entry close-up) shows a mismatched patched vertical strip of brick along the left door jamb with smeared, off-tone mortar, whitish staining/efflorescence on the brick faces, and a darker parged base treatment contrasting with the brick above; photo_001 (street view of #3227) shows tonal mottling across the brick field, soiling under the projecting sills and cornice, and a whitish repainted band at the first-floor base. Weathering/discoloration is modest but real, matching the adjudicated v1.1 axes (claim exact, work warranted) and the billed claim text "brickwork weathering or discoloration with intact mortar".

The 2a prose did NOT omit this. Photo_001's prose contains the condition explicitly ("Brick and masonry need close inspection: There appear to be areas of aging/discoloration and possibly prior patching"), and photo_008's prose contains it twice over ("mortar joints look weathered/uneven in places" and "the darker foundation/parged area contrasts with the brick and appears patched"). What the prose did NOT contain is any hedge that would license a later stage to distort it — no claim of a uniform facade, no assertion the brick was sound. So pass_2a is ruled out: the condition survives in both readings.

Walking the rest of the ladder, no earlier rung fails. 2b produced matching bullets on both photos ("Brick masonry shows aging and discoloration." idx 5; "The lower masonry base treatment is darker than the brick and appears patched." idx 6), both joined by exact method. 2c kept both — they appear in p2c_surviving, not p2c_dropped. 2d resolved both to brick_weathered_or_discolored via exact_kind routing, and that is the same item the human graded "exact", so the resolution is not wrong. 2e kept both issues (both issue_ids are in kept_issue_ids), and per the corpus rule 2e is not an available attribution regardless. Condition projection succeeded: both issues carry projected_condition_id oc1_261de865e0dd299d, so the condition existed and reached Terra.

Terra is therefore the first stage that went wrong. It returned verdict "unsupported" with the rationale "The visible brick facade appears generally uniform, with mortar joints intact and no clear weathering or discoloration," which drove disposition "excluded" and reason_code "verdict_unsupported". That rationale contradicts what the photos show, and it also misuses the claim's own wording: "with intact mortar" is part of the catalog claim's definition, not a fact that argues against it, so Terra cited a satisfied condition as grounds for rejection. This is not the post-Terra routing gap — Terra did not support the condition and then lose it downstream; Terra affirmatively rejected it, which is a rung the ladder covers.

To a renovator, this reads as a **dated, compact bathroom needing at least a cosmetic gut-and-refresh**, with a few items worth investigating before pricing:

- **Very tight layout:** The vanity, toilet, and tub crowd the room. Replacing the vanity with a narrower or wall-hung unit could materially improve clearance. Layout changes may be limited without moving plumbing.
- **Aged tub/shower surround:** The one-piece surround looks old and somewhat worn/discolored, especially around the tub base and seams. Check carefully for cracked caulk, soft walls/flooring, leaks, and subfloor damage before deciding whether refinishing is enough versus replacement.
- **Flooring is a concern:** The sheet/vinyl floor looks heavily stained and aged, particularly at the tub edge and around the vanity/toilet. That is a common location for hidden moisture damage.
- **Vanity is undersized and dated:** Basic small cabinet, exposed side gap, and an awkward sink/faucet setup. Easy visual upgrade, but inspect the wall and plumbing behind it.
- **Mirror/wall finish need work:** The mirror appears old and possibly deteriorated around the edges; walls have scuffs, patching, and an uneven/unfinished look. Fresh moisture-resistant paint, a proper vanity light, and new mirror would change the room quickly.
- **Electrical should be evaluated:** The visible receptacle appears dated; bathrooms generally need GFCI-protected outlet(s). Have an electrician verify grounding, GFCI protection, placement, and any needed ventilation wiring.
- **Ventilation is not apparent:** No exhaust fan is visible. Confirm one exists and vents outdoors; if not, adding one is important for long-term moisture control.
- **Toilet and trim are dated:** The toilet, baseboards, door hardware, and shower rod/curtain setup all signal a full finish-package update.

**Likely scope:** remove flooring and vanity, inspect for water damage, update GFCI/lighting/ventilation as needed, recaulk or replace the tub surround, install new flooring, vanity, toilet, trim, mirror, and paint.

The biggest unknown—and the cost driver—is **what is hiding under the flooring and behind the tub/vanity**, rather than the visible finishes.

- **Cabinets appear reusable:** They look generally intact and reasonably aligned. A budget renovation could include repainting/refacing, new pulls, soft-close hardware, and possibly replacing a few worn doors rather than a full cabinet tear-out.
- **Countertops are a major visual weakness:** The dark speckled laminate looks serviceable but dated and has limited backsplash integration. Replacing counters and adding a full-height tile backsplash would make a substantial difference.
- **Awkward corner storage:** The open curved corner shelving near the range is inefficient and visually busy. A renovator may consider a proper corner cabinet solution, pantry pull-outs, or a redesigned base-cabinet run.
- **Appliance package needs updating:** The white coil-top stove and older microwave are likely candidates for replacement. The kitchen would benefit visually from coordinated stainless or black appliances—assuming electrical/venting allows.
- **Range hood/venting is a key due-diligence item:** It appears to be a basic recirculating hood. Confirm whether it vents outdoors; adding exterior venting can be a meaningful upgrade and cost variable.
- **Flooring is ripe for replacement:** The vinyl is worn-looking and visually dated. LVP, tile, or a continuous floor into adjoining spaces would modernize it quickly.
- **Limited prep space:** The sink-side counter is crowded, and the dining table consumes much of the room. A layout rethink—smaller table, peninsula, or better storage—could improve usability if dimensions permit.
- **Window treatment and wall color are easy wins:** The floral valance/blinds and beige walls are purely cosmetic and inexpensive to modernize.
- **Potential concern to inspect:** The lower cabinetry/base areas, around the sink, and the floor near appliances should be checked for water damage, swelling, soft spots, or hidden leaks. Nothing severe is obvious in the photo, but these are typical risk zones.

**Bottom line:** This does not immediately look like a full gut-job from the photo. It looks like a strong candidate for a **mid-level kitchen refresh**—flooring, counters, backsplash, lighting, appliances, paint, hardware, and selective cabinet work—with a full remodel only if the owner wants to improve layout, storage, and ventilation.

Premise holds on my own inspection: all three photos show genuinely dated interior trim. photo_022 has heavy dark-stained casings on the cased opening and doorway plus mismatched baseboards and painted-over paneled doors; photo_028 has wide taupe-painted window casings with chipped, uneven paint and tired baseboards; photo_029 has aged painted paneled doors, jambs and casing. The 2a prose DID contain the condition on every evidence photo, so pass_2a is excluded: photo_022 lists "heavy dark wood trim, painted-over/dated doors, mismatched baseboards ... ready for modernization"; photo_028 has a whole bullet "Dated, rough window trim" describing wide painted trim with wear, uneven paint, gaps and minor damage; photo_029 has "doors and jambs look aged and may need adjustment, stripping, repainting, or replacement". What 2a did NOT contain is any statement that the trim is thin or builder-grade — it consistently describes substantial, heavy, wide, original trim.

Downstream, nothing was lost until Terra. 2b produced matching bullets and all three issues joined exactly (bullet_index 4, 9, 3, method exact). 2c kept all three (p2c_present true; the drops on these photos are unrelated bullets like windows, ceilings and the fire extinguisher). 2d resolved all three to dated_interior_trim by exact_kind — the item id matches the observation, and the adjudicated claim axis of "exact" forecloses calling this a wrong-item resolution. Condition projection succeeded: all three issues carry projected_condition_id oc1_c6c4c4017b1ed9dd, which reached Terra. 2e is not available here and in any case cost nothing (removed_count 0, condition projected despite p2e_status "absent"). Terra then returned verdict "unsupported" with reason_code verdict_unsupported, and the condition went unbilled (accepted false). Terra is therefore the first stage where a real, correctly-carried condition was destroyed.

Confidence is medium rather than high because of the misnamed-catalog tension: the billed claim_text is "interior trim plain, thin, or builder-grade trim package", and the trim in these photos is emphatically NOT thin or builder-grade, so Terra's rationale is literally accurate against the wording it was given. To a renovator, this reads as a **functional but dated kitchen with a clear cosmetic-to-moderate renovation opportunity**.

- **No visible backsplash:** There is an easy value-add opportunity for tile or a durable slab backsplash after countertop work.
- **Lighting is minimal:** A single flush-mount ceiling fixture is likely inadequate for a kitchen. Recessed lights, a brighter central fixture, and under-cabinet lighting would help considerably.
- **Flooring transition/condition:** The dark plank flooring in the kitchen contrasts with the carpeted adjacent area. It appears newer than the cabinetry but should be checked for moisture damage, soft spots, and installation quality—especially near the sink and refrigerator.
- **Potential layout opportunity:** The kitchen appears narrow but open toward an adjacent hall/living area. Depending on what is behind the walls, a renovator may look at widening the opening, adding a peninsula, or improving the visual connection to the next room.
- **Walls/ceilings:** Paint is dated but the surfaces do not show obvious major cracking in this photo. Still inspect for water staining, ventilation issues, and wall damage behind cabinets/appliances.

Overall: it looks like a **good candidate for a mid-level kitchen refresh**, with the main unknowns being plumbing, electrical, flooring condition, and whether the existing layout can be opened up without structural work.

- **Wall/trim quality:** Baseboards, caulking, and paint lines look incomplete or rough, suggesting this bathroom may have been partially updated without a full finish-out.

Overall, it reads as a **small, inexpensive cosmetic renovation with a need for careful plumbing/subfloor inspection**. The layout—not the finishes—is the main long-term limitation.

What the prose did NOT do is use wear vocabulary (no "scuffs", "paint loss", "dents") — it framed the trim as unfinished/rough rather than worn. So 2a is not the first failure: the observation is present and the photo supports it.

Every intermediate rung is clean. 2b produced the matching bullet verbatim (index 15, exact join). 2c kept it (it is in p2c_surviving as issue ee846d364a0b6a80, not in p2c_dropped). 2d resolved it to baseboard_wear_scuffs via exact_kind routing — and since the human graded the resulting claim axis "exact", that catalog item is a correct fit, so 2d did not mis-resolve. 2e kept the issue (p2e_status "kept", id present in kept_issue_ids), and per the case framing 2e cost nothing here anyway. condition_projection produced oc1_b10d0b1346b9e17a, so the condition existed and reached Terra.

Terra is therefore the first stage that went wrong: it returned terra_verdict "unsupported" with the rationale "The visible baseboards do not show clear scuffs, paint loss, dents, or general wear," and that verdict is what unbilled the condition (disposition "excluded", reason_code "verdict_unsupported"). prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise confirmed by direct inspection: masonry weathering/discoloration is plainly real across this property, and it is not only stone. photo_023 shows a genuine BRICK Tudor house whose tall brick chimney stack carries heavy dark vertical staining, plus a brick retaining wall and a stained/parged wall below the porch; photo_014 and photo_034 show a sandstone facade and chimney with dark staining, biological growth and worn joints; photo_035 shows discolored/moss-stained stone with patched mortar; photo_002/photo_022 show a heavily moss-stained, spalled masonry grill. The condition "brickwork weathering or discoloration" is supported, and the human adjudication (claim=exact, work=warranted) is the authority here.

The 2a prose is not the failure point: it contains the condition explicitly on four of the six photos — photo_014 "Heavy staining/weathering and potentially deteriorated mortar joints", photo_023 "The tall brick stack shows weathering", photo_034 "the chimney and some wall areas show dark staining, weathering", photo_035 "There appear to be patched/repointed areas, discoloration". What 2a did NOT contain is any claim that the mortar is intact — it repeatedly said the opposite (deteriorated/uneven mortar joints, repointing needed) — but that is a detail of the catalog item's claim wording, not an absence of the condition.

Every later stage carried it forward intact: all seven issues joined to a 2b bullet by exact match, all seven survived 2c (p2c_present true), 2d resolved each to brick_weathered_or_discolored via exact_kind, all were kept by 2e, and all seven projected to the single condition oc1_fd62a1d71743be6b, which reached Terra. So 2b, 2c, 2d, condition_projection and 2e all did their job (and per the record 2e never costs a condition in this corpus).

Terra is the first and only stage that went wrong: it returned "unsupported" on a condition whose substance it conceded — "The visible masonry is heavily stained and weathered, but it is stone rather than brick and some joints appear deteriorated" — rejecting on the catalog item's material/mortar wording rather than on whether the weathering exists. That rejection is what unbilled it (accepted=false, reason_code verdict_unsupported, disposition excluded), and photo_023 shows actual brick with weathering and intact mortar, so even the literal wording had support. This is not the post-Terra routing gap: Terra did not support the condition, it rejected it.

I considered 2d — picking a brick-named item for evidence that is mostly stone is what set Terra's objection up — but the adjudicated truth basis records the claim axis as "exact", meaning the resolved item's claim matches the photos, so 2d did not go wrong by the governing authority.

photo_001.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely notice:

- **Strong original rowhouse character:** The red-brick façade, arched window heads, brownstone/stone base, projecting window sills, and ornate cornice/brackets are valuable period details worth preserving.
- **Good curb-appeal upside:** The basic façade reads more intact and cohesive than many heavily altered rowhomes. A restrained restoration—cleaning/repointing brick, repainting trim, upgraded door/lighting—could have a major payoff.
- **Brick and masonry need close inspection:** There appear to be areas of aging/discoloration and possibly prior patching. Check mortar condition, lintels/arches, settlement cracks, moisture entry, and whether any brick has been painted or improperly repointed.
- **Cornice/roofline is a key risk item:** The decorative metal/wood cornice looks largely present, but these can hide rot, corrosion, loose elements, and roof-edge drainage problems. Inspect from the roof rather than judging from this view alone.
- **Mixed/older windows:** Some windows look like older replacement units or varying styles. They may be serviceable, but a renovation should consider energy performance, air sealing, and retaining/restoring the historically prominent openings where feasible.
- **Basement-level opportunity and concern:** The visible lower-level windows suggest usable basement space, but also raise questions about waterproofing, ceiling height, egress, foundation condition, and whether it can legally be finished or rented.
- **Entry needs modernization:** The red door is a visual focal point but the stoop, railings, landing, house-number/mailbox setup, and exterior light could be upgraded for a cleaner, higher-end first impression.
- **Street tree is both asset and maintenance issue:** It softens the frontage but obscures the house and may contribute leaves/gutter clogging or root-related sidewalk issues. Pruning and checking sidewalk/root conditions would be sensible.
- **Tight attached-house renovation realities:** Any structural, plumbing, electrical, roof, or drainage work needs coordination with adjoining properties and careful party-wall assessment.

From this exterior alone, it looks more like a **character-preserving renovation with targeted envelope and systems work** than a façade needing wholesale rebuilding. The biggest unknowns are roof/cornice condition, rear façade condition, water intrusion, basement condition, and interior mechanicals.

prior_attribution.p2a_excerpt: visible waviness/sagging around the porch-roof connection
prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise confirmed by inspection: photo_001.jpg shows a full-width covered porch whose roof fascia/soffit line is visibly wavy rather than straight, with a dark ragged band of out-of-plane, deteriorated boards where the porch roof meets the main house above the steps. That is consistent with the adjudicated v1.1 axes (claim=exact, work=warranted), so the condition is real and the pipeline failed to bill it.

The 2a prose DID contain the condition, in plain terms: under "Roof condition" it states the shingles look aged and uneven "with visible waviness/sagging around the porch-roof connection," and separately notes the porch's "fascia, railings, steps, and porch roof appear weathered" and "may need substantial carpentry work-not just paint." What the 2a prose did NOT contain is the specific vocabulary of the catalog item ("soffit," "porch ceiling panels," "loose or missing panels") -- it described the same physical defect at the porch-roof connection in roof/framing language rather than soffit language. That wording gap did not cost anything downstream: 2b lifted the sentence verbatim as bullet index 1 (exact join), 2c kept it (p2c_present true, and the only 2c drops on this photo are four benign non-defect bullets: low house, flat yard, large porch, mature trees), 2d resolved it via the llm path to soffit_or_porch_ceiling_failed on exact_kind routing -- a resolution the human's "exact" claim axis explicitly ratifies, so 2d is not the fault -- 2e kept the issue (p2e_status kept, issue id present in kept_issue_ids), and condition_projection produced oc1_69263601050587ce.

So the condition survived intact all the way to the final verdict, and the first and only stage that went wrong is terra: it returned cannot_assess with the rationale that "the porch ceiling or soffit panels are not clearly visible enough to judge sagging, looseness, or missing panels," which set accepted=false with reason_code verdict_cannot_assess. Terra's non-assessment is what dropped a claim the human found exactly supported and warranted, on a photo where the sagging porch-roof/soffit line is in fact discernible. This is NOT the known post-Terra routing gap: that gap applies only when Terra SUPPORTED the condition and disposition still unbilled it. Here Terra did not support it -- cannot_assess is itself the terminal non-accept -- so the ladder has a rung that fits, and the "inspection" disposition is a consequence of Terra's verdict rather than an independent routing decision. The 2e note in the record (one tier_optional_suppressed count on this photo) is a red herring per the stated corpus rule and, in any case, this issue was kept and projected.

per_issue.observation: Vinyl flooring is worn-looking and visually dated.

photo_005.jpg.p2a_prose:
To a renovator, this reads as a **functional but dated kitchen with a fairly contained cosmetic-refresh opportunity**.

**What stands out:**

- **Original/older layout and finishes:** Raised-panel white cabinets, laminate counters, small mosaic backsplash, vinyl sheet flooring, fluorescent-style range hood, and electric coil range all date the room.
- **Cabinets appear reusable:** They look generally intact and reasonably aligned. A budget renovation could include repainting/refacing, new pulls, soft-close hardware, and possibly replacing a few worn doors rather than a full cabinet tear-out.
- **Countertops are a major visual weakness:** The dark speckled laminate looks serviceable but dated and has limited backsplash integration. Replacing counters and adding a full-height tile backsplash would make a substantial difference.
- **Awkward corner storage:** The open curved corner shelving near the range is inefficient and visually busy. A renovator may consider a proper corner cabinet solution, pantry pull-outs, or a redesigned base-cabinet run.
- **Appliance package needs updating:** The white coil-top stove and older microwave are likely candidates for replacement. The kitchen would benefit visually from coordinated stainless or black appliances—assuming electrical/venting allows.
- **Range hood/venting is a key due-diligence item:** It appears to be a basic recirculating hood. Confirm whether it vents outdoors; adding exterior venting can be a meaningful upgrade and cost variable.
- **Flooring is ripe for replacement:** The vinyl is worn-looking and visually dated. LVP, tile, or a continuous floor into adjoining spaces would modernize it quickly.
- **Limited prep space:** The sink-side counter is crowded, and the dining table consumes much of the room. A layout rethink—smaller table, peninsula, or better storage—could improve usability if dimensions permit.
- **Window treatment and wall color are easy wins:** The floral valance/blinds and beige walls are purely cosmetic and inexpensive to modernize.
- **Potential concern to inspect:** The lower cabinetry/base areas, around the sink, and the floor near appliances should be checked for water damage, swelling, soft spots, or hidden leaks. Nothing severe is obvious in the photo, but these are typical risk zones.

**Bottom line:** This does not immediately look like a full gut-job from the photo. It looks like a strong candidate for a **mid-level kitchen refresh**—flooring, counters, backsplash, lighting, appliances, paint, hardware, and selective cabinet work—with a full remodel only if the owner wants to improve layout, storage, and ventilation.

prior_attribution.p2a_excerpt: The vinyl is worn-looking and visually dated. LVP, tile, or a continuous floor into adjoining spaces would modernize it quickly.
prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise holds. Photo_005 is a dated kitchen: white raised-panel cabinets, dark speckled laminate counters, mosaic backsplash, coil range, and a beige faux-tile-pattern vinyl SHEET floor running under the range and dining table. The floor reads as intact and unbroken -- no tears, no discrete stains, no visible discoloration beyond general dinginess/scuffing near the range toe-kick -- but its pattern and material plainly date the room and it is a legitimate replacement item. That is exactly the human adjudication: work=warranted, claim=misnamed. So a real condition existed and went unbilled (disposition excluded, reason verdict_unsupported) -- a MISS.

Pass 2a is NOT at fault: the prose carries the condition with the correct meaning, in the "Flooring is ripe for replacement" bullet -- "The vinyl is worn-looking and visually dated. LVP, tile, or a continuous floor into adjoining spaces would modernize it quickly." The framing there is modernization (dated, replace to modernize), with "worn-looking" used as an appearance word, not a claim of staining or material failure. 2b rendered it faithfully as bullet 13, "Vinyl flooring is worn-looking and visually dated." (exact join), and 2c kept it -- it is present in p2c_surviving, so neither of those rungs fits.

2d is the first stage that went wrong. With 7 candidates it took resolution_path=lexical_shortcut on shortcut_reason=support_phrase_hit -- i.e. it latched onto the token "worn" -- and resolved to the degradation item vinyl_linoleum_worn_or_stained, whose claim text asserts "vinyl or linoleum flooring staining, discoloration, or wear on intact material." That is a physical-deterioration assertion the prose never made and the photo does not support, and it discards the half of the bullet that actually mattered ("visually dated"). The same photo's other dated-finish bullets resolved correctly to modernization items (outdated_kitchen_finishes, appliances_dated_or_basic), which is where a dated-flooring observation belonged. Condition projection then faithfully carried the misnamed claim forward, and Terra rejected it accurately on its own terms -- "The visible vinyl flooring appears intact without clear staining, discoloration, or wear" -- which matches what I see in the photo. Terra therefore is not the first wrong stage; it verified correctly the claim it was handed. One caveat: the record exposes catalog kind only alongside the 2d-resolved item, so if the degradation kind label were assigned upstream at 2c rather than chosen at 2d, blame would shift one rung earlier; the recorded p2d shortcut mechanism is the concrete documented cause, so 2d is the call.

A renovator would likely flag this as a **solid “bones, but exterior-heavy” project**:

- **Roof and porch roof:** Main roof appears aged/weathered; the lower porch/awning roof looks patched and may have sagging or deteriorated fascia/trim. Budget for close inspection and possible replacement.
- **Siding/trim condition:** Painted wood siding has visible wear, uneven boards/patching, and tired trim details—likely prep, repairs, and repainting at minimum; check for rot behind it.
- **Windows:** A mix of window styles/sizes, including older units and a glass-block-style window, creates an inconsistent façade. Window upgrades could improve efficiency and resale appeal, but may require reframing/trim work.
- **Front entry/porch:** The recessed porch/entry has minimal curb appeal, worn decking, and a makeshift feel. Reworking this area could make the biggest visual impact.
- **Exterior drainage/foundation check:** The low roofline, limited visible gutters/downspout routing, and grade near the house warrant checking for water management, foundation moisture, and basement issues.
- **Landscaping and site cleanup:** Overgrown trees/shrubs obscure the house, and the stump plus worn walkway reduce appeal. Clearing, pruning, a new path, and basic grading would be relatively high-return improvements.
- **Potential layout/structural quirks:** The irregular window placement and apparent additions suggest confirming interior flow, permits, and whether walls/roof transitions have been properly detailed.

Overall, it reads as a property where **roofing, exterior envelope, windows, porch redesign, and landscaping** could materially transform value—provided inspection does not uncover moisture, foundation, or structural issues.

prior_attribution.p2a_excerpt: Painted wood siding, trim, and fascia look weathered in places. Expect prep/repair and repainting at minimum
prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise confirmed by my own inspection. Both photos show the same older house clad in white painted wood siding whose finish is plainly tired: in photo_006 (flat overcast light) the paint reads dingy with a gray cast and streaking across the second story below the roofline, soiling on the wall under the porch roof, and a duller, grayer tone on the lower-level wall than the upper; photo_019 (harsh summer sun, more flattering) still shows mottled gray, uneven tone on the shaded elevation and along the lower courses. That matches the adjudicated v1.1 axes (claim exact, work warranted) for the claim "exterior siding finish fading, chalking, or uneven discoloration."

The 2a prose did NOT miss this. photo_006's prose states the painted wood siding "has visible wear, uneven boards/patching, and tired trim details" and calls for "prep, repairs, and repainting at minimum"; photo_019's prose states the painted wood siding, trim and fascia "look weathered in places" and again expects "prep/repair and repainting at minimum." What the 2a prose did not do is use the narrower vocabulary of fading/chalking/discoloration — it described the same finish failure as wear/weathering. That distinction is the only thing that could have pushed the fault earlier to 2d (a wrong-item resolution from "weathered" to "discoloration_fading"), but the human adjudicated the resulting claim text as EXACT, which means the catalog item 2d chose was the right one for what the photos show. So 2d is not the first failure either.

Everything downstream of 2a ran clean: all three issues joined to 2b bullets by exact match (indices 4, 6, 7), all three survived 2c, all three resolved to exterior_siding_discoloration_fading via exact_kind, all three carry p2e_status "kept", and all three projected to condition oc1_b2e96c2b1020d48b, which reached Terra. Terra then returned verdict "unsupported" with the rationale that the visible white siding "does not show clear fading, chalking, or uneven discoloration," and that verdict alone produced reason_code verdict_unsupported and the unbilled outcome. Terra is therefore the first stage that went wrong: it rejected a condition that the pipeline had correctly observed, structured, filtered, resolved and projected, and that the photos support. This is not the known post-Terra routing gap, because Terra did not support the condition and lose it to disposition — Terra itself is the rejecting stage.

per_issue.observation: The shower valve and trim appear damaged.

photo_017.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely see this as a **full-gut bathroom**, not a cosmetic refresh.

- **Clear moisture/water damage:** Deteriorated wall material around and beneath the sink/toilet, staining at the shower curb and floor, and possible mold or rot indications. The source and extent need investigation before finishes go in.
- **Plumbing concerns:** Exposed, aged drain/supply lines under the sink; the shower valve/trim appears incomplete or damaged. Budget for updating supply, drains, shutoffs, and potentially venting.
- **Shower needs rebuilding:** The shower looks unfinished or heavily compromised, with a questionable curb/pan condition and old wall tile. Assume demolition to framing/subfloor and a new properly waterproofed pan and surround.
- **Old finishes throughout:** Dated tile, damaged flooring, worn fixtures, old medicine cabinet, mirror/light area, and likely several layers of prior patchwork.
- **Electrical/ventilation should be checked:** The fixture area looks outdated, and there is no obvious exhaust fan. A remodel should include GFCI-protected outlets, modern lighting, and venting to the exterior.
- **Potential hidden structural/subfloor work:** The staining and deterioration at the floor-wall junction make subfloor, framing, and toilet flange condition important inspection items.

The upside is that it appears to be a compact, straightforward layout with the core fixtures already grouped together, so keeping the general footprint could control costs. But I’d price it as demolition, remediation, plumbing/electrical review, waterproofing, and complete replacement—not simply new tile and paint.

prior_attribution.p2a_excerpt: The shower looks unfinished or heavily compromised, with a questionable curb/pan condition and old wall tile.
prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise confirmed on my own reading of photo_017.jpg: the shower's wet-area enclosure is genuinely damaged — the tile wall is broken open at the valve location (rough, chipped penetration, no trim/escutcheon), there is a second damaged penetration at the bare shower-arm stub, and the mud pan and curb are eroded, spalled and chipped under heavy staining. That matches the claim text "tub surround or shower pan cracked, chipped, or damaged wet-area enclosure" and matches the v1.1 adjudication (claim=exact, work=warranted). The condition was projected (oc1_c00cb1e0f1fdb9da) and then unbilled with disposition=excluded / reason_code=verdict_unsupported, so it is a miss.

Walking the ladder: 2a DID contain the condition — the prose names the enclosure twice ("a questionable curb/pan condition", "a new properly waterproofed pan and surround") and separately notes "the shower valve/trim appears incomplete or damaged". What the prose did not contain was the literal words "cracked" or "chipped"; it hedged the enclosure as "questionable" and "heavily compromised", but the condition is unmistakably present, so 2a is not the failure. 2b emitted the matching bullet and joined it exactly (bullet_index 4, method exact). 2c kept it (p2c_present true); it dropped the sibling bullet "The shower curb and pan condition is questionable.", but that drop cost nothing because the surviving bullet carried the same condition forward. 2d resolved to tub_surround_or_shower_pan_damage — the bullet is phrased about valve/trim while the item is about the enclosure, which is the one arguable hop, but the human adjudicated the resulting claim as EXACT, so by the truth basis 2d resolved correctly and is not the first wrong stage. 2e kept the issue, and per the record 2e never cost a condition here. condition_projection produced the condition and it reached Terra.

Terra is therefore the first stage that went wrong: it returned "unsupported" with the rationale that only staining was visible and "no clear crack, chip, or enclosure damage is visible", which the photo contradicts — the surround is physically broken open at two wall penetrations and the pan/curb is chipped and degraded. Terra's rejection is what caused the unbilling (reason_code verdict_unsupported), so this is a Terra verdict error, not the known post-Terra routing/disposition gap (that gap applies only when Terra supported the condition).

- **Flooring transition/condition:** The dark plank flooring in the kitchen contrasts with the carpeted adjacent area. It appears newer than the cabinetry but should be checked for moisture damage, soft spots, and installation quality—especially near the sink and refrigerator.
- **Potential layout opportunity:** The kitchen appears narrow but open toward an adjacent hall/living area. Depending on what is behind the walls, a renovator may look at widening the opening, adding a peninsula, or improving the visual connection to the next room.
- **Walls/ceilings:** Paint is dated but the surfaces do not show obvious major cracking in this photo. Still inspect for water staining, ventilation issues, and wall damage behind cabinets/appliances.

photo_004.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely see this as a **full kitchen gut/refresh opportunity**, with some promising layout features but clear deferred maintenance.

**Immediate standouts**
- **Very dated kitchen**: older cabinetry, laminate counters, freestanding electric range, and an awkward/open lower cabinet area. Most buyers would expect replacement rather than cosmetic touch-up.
- **Flooring is a major issue**: worn, stained/discolored sheet flooring or old vinyl/linoleum with visible seams and damage. Plan on removal and subfloor inspection before new flooring.
- **Wall condition**: scuffs, holes, patches, and apparent old adhesive/fixture marks suggest prep work—patching, skim coating as needed, priming, and repainting.
- **Ceiling/finish quality**: ceiling looks aged/discolored and may need repainting; inspect around the light and exterior wall/window for any moisture-related staining or deterioration.
- **Cabinet and counter condition**: painted cabinets appear tired, with dated hardware and likely limited functional storage. The sink base and lower cabinets deserve a close inspection for water damage.
- **Electrical/lighting modernization**: the ceiling fixture is dated, and visible low wall wiring/cords under the left counter area raise questions about outlets, circuits, and code-compliant kitchen electrical. An electrician should evaluate.
- **Window and exterior door**: both look older and may be drafty; check operability, framing, flashing, and any signs of water intrusion.
- **Layout potential**: it is a long, workable galley-style room with a window and exterior access. A renovation could add a continuous cabinet run, better pantry storage, modern appliances, improved lighting, and possibly a small eat-in or prep zone along the left wall.

**What to investigate before pricing the job**
1. Condition of subfloor/floor joists under the existing floor.
2. Plumbing age and condition under the sink and behind the range wall.
3. Electrical panel capacity, grounded outlets, GFCI protection, and range circuit.
4. Whether the exterior wall/window area has moisture, mold, or insulation issues.
5. Ventilation: no obvious range hood is visible, so confirm whether one can be vented outside.
6. Lead/asbestos testing as appropriate for an older property before demolition.

In short: **not a simple paint-and-appliance update**—budget as a substantial kitchen renovation, while recognizing the room has usable dimensions and a straightforward layout to improve.

- **Open shelving/window wall:** this is a visual liability now, but could become a feature—new window treatment, drywall/trim repair, or a redesigned sink/window zone could improve it substantially.

photo_005.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely see a **clean, functional but dated bathroom with a strong “cosmetic-update” opportunity** rather than an obvious full gut requirement.

**What stands out:**
- **Narrow/linear layout:** Tub/shower, toilet, and vanity are tightly arranged, so moving plumbing may not be worthwhile unless a larger reconfiguration is planned.
- **Dated shower enclosure:** The textured sliding glass doors and metal framing are a clear age marker. Replacing them with a cleaner frameless/semi-frameless panel or a new tub surround would modernize the room quickly.
- **Builder-grade vanity and top:** White cabinet is serviceable, but the beige integrated sink/counter, small knobs, and traditional faucet date it. A new vanity top, faucet, hardware, and possibly vanity would have high visual impact.
- **Old-school mirrored medicine cabinet/light bar:** The multi-bulb “Hollywood” fixture and large mirrored cabinet are prime upgrade targets. Better vanity lighting and a framed mirror or modern recessed cabinet would change the feel significantly.
- **Floor tile/grout:** Beige ceramic tile appears intact but reads dated; grout condition and soundness should be checked. New large-format porcelain or LVP-rated-for-bath use could refresh it, though floor height and toilet reset need consideration.
- **Window/privacy:** Good natural light is a plus, but the blind and window trim look dated. A moisture-resistant privacy treatment or frosted film may be preferable; verify the window is well sealed given its proximity to wet areas.
- **Ventilation:** There appears to be a ceiling exhaust grille. A renovator would test whether it actually vents outdoors and has adequate airflow—important before investing in finishes.
- **Potential hidden-risk areas:** Inspect tub surround, shower-door tracks, caulk, floor perimeter, vanity base, and around the window for moisture damage. Nothing obvious is visible in the photo, but these are the likely trouble spots.

**Best value scope:** retain the existing layout; update shower enclosure/surround, vanity/top/faucet, lighting/mirror, flooring, paint, and accessories. A full remodel would mainly be justified if inspections reveal water damage or the goal is to enlarge/improve the shower experience.

A renovator would likely notice:

- **Awkward bedroom geometry:** The room is long and narrow, with a projecting/curved soffit or bulkhead along the right side and a beam across the ceiling. It limits furniture placement and makes the space feel more like a converted or reconfigured area than a clean rectangular bedroom.
- **Potentially low/uneven ceiling conditions:** The ceiling drops and boxed-in areas deserve investigation—could simply conceal HVAC, plumbing, or structure, but should be understood before opening walls.
- **Odd door/transom setup:** The closet door with the large transom-like opening above it, plus the nearby open doorway, creates visual clutter. A remodel could simplify this with a full-height closet system, revised door placement, or more cohesive trim.
- **Limited usable wall space:** The windows, closet, hall opening, and unusual ceiling leave relatively little uninterrupted wall area. Built-ins or a more deliberate furniture layout may add value.
- **Dated finishes:** Carpet, basic trim, flush-panel closet door, and the ceiling light fixture are straightforward cosmetic upgrade opportunities.

- **Counters and backsplash are not fully coordinated**: The veined stone counters and white subway tile are functional, but the mix feels somewhat piecemeal against the ornate ceiling. Upgrading the countertop/backsplash pairing could make the room feel more designed.
- **Lighting is a design opportunity**: The industrial pendants complement the dark ceiling, but the room could benefit from layered task lighting—especially under-cabinet lighting—and possibly a more balanced fixture plan.

prior_attribution.rationale:
Premise holds. All three photos show the same living/entry space of what reads as a recently flipped house: fresh gray walls, new white baseboards and casing, a new entry door with beveled glass, and hardwood in a deep uniform reddish-brown stain at a high, even gloss. I looked specifically for the billed condition (hard_flooring_scratched_or_worn: "scratches, scuffs, or worn finish on intact flooring") and found none of it — no scratch tracks, no scuffed traffic lanes, no dulled or clouded patches, no finish loss at the door thresholds or the room transitions. The floors look newly refinished. What the model appears to have read as wear is specular reflection: photo_004 and photo_025 both have a large window bank throwing a bright glare band across the boards, and photo_032 has strong side light from the left window wall, so the floor is bright where it reflects the windows and dark where it does not. That is a lighting artifact and normal oak grain/color variation between boards, not finish condition. Terra's rationale ("visible scuffing and uneven sheen in multiple areas") repeats the same misread rather than correcting it.

The error is already fully present at 2a and originates there. Each photo's 2a prose asserts the wear in its own words while otherwise praising the floor: photo_004 "the hardwood appears continuous and generally serviceable, though it has visible wear/sheen variation"; photo_025 "there are visible scuffs/wear and possibly some uneven coloration"; photo_032 "they look dark and somewhat worn/uneven in sheen." So the unsupported material claim — that the finish is scuffed/worn — is authored by the VLM read of the pixels, not introduced later. Every downstream stage merely carried it faithfully: 2b restated it near-verbatim as a bullet on each photo (all three joined "exact"), 2c let it survive, 2d resolved it to the matching catalog item hard_flooring_scratched_or_worn via exact_kind, 2e kept all three issues, and condition_projection merged them into the single condition oc1_80bb9450d428a649. No stage after 2a distorted, strengthened, or invented anything; each one is a faithful transformation of a claim that was false when it entered the pipeline. That makes 2a the first stage that went wrong.

Confidence is medium rather than higher for two reasons: the truth basis is a single collapsed v1 verdict that was never re-adjudicated, and "worn with uneven sheen" is a soft, hedged claim of the kind a careful reviewer could argue toward from the glare bands, even though on inspection I do not think the pixels support it.

Premise confirmed by inspection: photo_001.jpg shows a full-width covered porch whose roof fascia/soffit line is visibly wavy rather than straight, with a dark ragged band of out-of-plane, deteriorated boards where the porch roof meets the main house above the steps. That is consistent with the adjudicated v1.1 axes (claim=exact, work=warranted), so the condition is real and the pipeline failed to bill it.

The 2a prose DID contain the condition, in plain terms: under "Roof condition" it states the shingles look aged and uneven "with visible waviness/sagging around the porch-roof connection," and separately notes the porch's "fascia, railings, steps, and porch roof appear weathered" and "may need substantial carpentry work-not just paint." What the 2a prose did NOT contain is the specific vocabulary of the catalog item ("soffit," "porch ceiling panels," "loose or missing panels") -- it described the same physical defect at the porch-roof connection in roof/framing language rather than soffit language. That wording gap did not cost anything downstream: 2b lifted the sentence verbatim as bullet index 1 (exact join), 2c kept it (p2c_present true, and the only 2c drops on this photo are four benign non-defect bullets: low house, flat yard, large porch, mature trees), 2d resolved it via the llm path to soffit_or_porch_ceiling_failed on exact_kind routing -- a resolution the human's "exact" claim axis explicitly ratifies, so 2d is not the fault -- 2e kept the issue (p2e_status kept, issue id present in kept_issue_ids), and condition_projection produced oc1_69263601050587ce.

So the condition survived intact all the way to the final verdict, and the first and only stage that went wrong is terra: it returned cannot_assess with the rationale that "the porch ceiling or soffit panels are not clearly visible enough to judge sagging, looseness, or missing panels," which set accepted=false with reason_code verdict_cannot_assess. Terra's non-assessment is what dropped a claim the human found exactly supported and warranted, on a photo where the sagging porch-roof/soffit line is in fact discernible. This is NOT the known post-Terra routing gap: that gap applies only when Terra SUPPORTED the condition and disposition still unbilled it. Here Terra did not support it -- cannot_assess is itself the terminal non-accept -- so the ladder has a rung that fits, and the "inspection" disposition is a consequence of Terra's verdict rather than an independent routing decision. The 2e note in the record (one tier_optional_suppressed count on this photo) is a red herring per the stated corpus rule and, in any case, this issue was kept and projected.

photo_002.jpg.p2a_prose:
A renovator would likely see a **full gut-or-major-refresh kitchen**, but also a workable footprint and plenty of upside.

**What stands out immediately:**
- **Very dated finishes:** raised-panel cabinets, laminate/parquet-style flooring, tile backsplash, soffit/upper cabinetry, old lighting, and the built-in wall oven/cooktop arrangement all read several decades old.
- **Worn cabinetry:** doors/drawers appear misaligned or damaged in places; the sink-base area especially looks tired and may have moisture wear. Plan on replacement rather than just cosmetic paint unless boxes prove sound.
- **Aging appliances/layout:** separate cooktop and wall oven, refrigerator sitting outside the main cabinet run, and limited clear counter space make the kitchen feel inefficient by current standards.
- **Potential water-risk area:** inspect closely under the sink, along the dishwasher/sink-side cabinets, and at the floor around the sink for soft spots, staining, rot, or subfloor damage.
- **Flooring condition:** heavily worn and likely needs removal. The floor should be checked once exposed, especially where there is visible discoloration/finish loss.
- **Lighting/electrical likely need updating:** pendant fixtures are dated, and there appear to be relatively few convenient task-lighting options. A renovation should account for recessed/task lighting, under-cabinet lighting, and updated outlets/GFCI protection.
- **Open shelving/window wall:** this is a visual liability now, but could become a feature—new window treatment, drywall/trim repair, or a redesigned sink/window zone could improve it substantially.

**Positive renovation signals:**
- The room has a reasonably efficient **U-/L-shaped work zone** with the sink, cooking area, and refrigerator fairly close together.
- There is meaningful cabinet volume and enough floor area for a compact dining table or potentially a more useful island/peninsula, depending on adjacent-room dimensions.
- The cabinet wall may allow a cleaner modern plan: full-height pantry storage, a standard range, relocated refrigerator, and longer uninterrupted counters.

**Likely scope:** At minimum, new flooring, cabinets or cabinet rehabilitation, countertops, sink/faucet, appliances, lighting, paint, and backsplash. A prudent buyer should budget for hidden plumbing, electrical, subfloor, and wall repairs until inspections/open-up confirm otherwise.

human_label.finding: Long concrete entry steps are weathered and stained

prior_attribution.rationale: 2a looked directly at the stair run and read it as sound rather than weathered: it says the run 'looks fairly substantial and generally serviceable from the photo', and the only follow-up it raises is prospective inspection for cracking, settlement, loose edges and handrail height -- i.e. hypothetical structural checks, not the observed surface condition. Nowhere in the prose is there any claim of weathering, staining, discoloration or soiling of the concrete, so there was no material claim for 2b to structure. The 2b bullet faithfully mirrors 2a ('The concrete stair run appears substantial and generally serviceable.'), which confirms nothing was lost after 2a. Downstream stages cannot be blamed for dropping a claim that was never made, so the first responsible stage is 2a itself. Caveat lowering confidence to medium: this record carries lineage for one photo only, and I cannot check whether another exterior photo's p2a_prose captured the stained treads -- the pass_2a rung strictly requires absence from ALL evidence photos. Secondary uncertainty: whether generic exterior concrete weathering is a billable v5 item or support-only wear.

That bullet appears verbatim in p2c_dropped, so the 2c filter removed a correct, actionable, foundation-moisture observation without any recorded rationale, and no drainage condition exists anywhere in conditions_on_photo as a result. Nothing after 2c ever had the chance to act, so 2c is unambiguously the first responsible stage. The physical claim is independently verified in the image (white corrugated extension terminating at grade beside the basement window), and downspout-at-foundation is standard exterior scope, so both the miss and its attribution are high confidence.

human_label.finding: Storm/screen door is dated

prior_attribution.p2a_excerpt: **Entry door/windows:** The entry door and storm/security treatment are clear modernization opportunities.
prior_attribution.rationale: 2a carried the material claim: the entry door and storm/security treatment are called 'clear modernization opportunities', which is precisely the gold finding. 2b then flattened that into a bare existence statement -- 'The entry door has storm or security treatment.' -- which asserts only that a storm door is present and drops the dated/modernization meaning entirely. That flattening is what doomed it: this photo gives a direct control for how 2c behaves, since 2c kept 'The porch guard and ironwork feel dated' (modifier intact) while dropping every neutral existence bullet, including this one. So 2c was acting on the degraded text 2b handed it, and the first stage that distorted the observation is 2b. Confidence is medium because the alternative reading is defensible: if one counts any bullet naming the same object as a 'matching 2b bullet', then the bullet was present and dropped, and the rung would be 2c instead.

human_label.finding: Metal step handrail is older with worn paint

prior_attribution.p2a_excerpt: **Handrail and safety:** The single narrow metal rail and porch guard/ironwork feel dated; replacing or refinishing them could improve both safety and appearance.
prior_attribution.rationale: 2a captured the rail as dated and refinish-worthy in a single sentence that yoked it to the porch ironwork. 2b split that sentence into two bullets and preserved the 'feel dated' modifier on only one of them: the porch-guard bullet kept it (and duly survived 2c, resolved to curb_appeal_upgrade, and was supported by Terra), while the stair-rail bullet was reduced to 'The stair rail is a single narrow metal rail.' -- pure geometry, no condition. The two bullets from one source sentence with opposite fates make 2b's asymmetric flattening the first responsible distortion; 2c's drop of the stripped bullet is consistent with its treatment of every other neutral bullet on this photo. Medium confidence for two reasons: the same present-object-vs-present-claim ambiguity as g6 would put this on 2c, and the finding partly overlaps the curb_appeal_upgrade condition, which Terra supported and post-Terra routing then set to no_action -- if one judges that condition to cover the stair rail, this case has no ladder rung at all and the honest answer would be unclear.
